etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schort, short, from Old English sċeort, sċort (“short”), from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.

definitions.definition: Having a small distance from one end or edge to another, either horizontally or vertically.
(of a person) Of comparatively small height.
Having little duration.

quote.citation: 2012 March-April, Anna Lena Phillips, “Sneaky Silk Moths”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 2, page 172:
quote.text: Last spring, the periodical cicadas emerged across eastern North America. Their vast numbers and short above-ground life spans inspired awe and irritation in humans—and made for good meals for birds and small mammals.

definitions.definition: (followed by for) Of a word or phrase, constituting an abbreviation (for another) or shortened form (of another).
(cricket, of a fielder or fielding position) that is relatively close to the batsman.
(cricket, of a ball) bowled so that it bounces relatively far from the batsman.
(golf, of an approach shot or putt) that falls short of the green or the hole.
(gambling) Of betting odds, offering a small return for the money wagered.
(baking, of pastries, metallurgy) Brittle, crumbly. (See shortbread, shortcake, shortcrust, shortening, hot short, cold-short.)

quote.text: I chose to interpret the references to butter and sugar as indicating that a short pastry was required. (Later editions suggest a biscuit-like texture.)

definitions.definition: Abrupt; brief; pointed; petulant.

quote.citation: 1870 April–September, Charles Dickens, The Mystery of Edwin Drood, London: Chapman and Hall, […], published 1870, →OCLC:
quote.text: “We are short to-night!” cries the woman, with a propitiatory laugh. “Short and snappish we are!  […] ”

definitions.definition: Limited in quantity; inadequate; insufficient; scanty.
Insufficiently provided; inadequately supplied, especially with money; scantily furnished; lacking.
Deficient; less; not coming up to a measure or standard.

quote.citation: 1829, Walter Savage Landor, “The Emperor Alexander and Capo D'Istria”, in Imaginary Conversations, volume IV:
quote.text: […] the people are worn down with taxes, and hardly anything short of an invasion could rouse them again to war.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) Undiluted; neat.

quote.citation: 1846 October 1 – 1848 April 1, Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: “There ain’t no drain of nothing short handy, is there?” said the Chicken, generally. “This here sluicing night is hard lines to a man as lives on his condition.”Captain Cuttle proffered a glass of rum  […]
Delance raised his beer and watched Hoadly throw down another swig of hard stuff. "Take it short if you want to make it over the mountain tonight."

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Not distant in time; near at hand.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 18:
quote.text: Marinell was sore offended / That his departure thence should be so short.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: He commanded those who were appointed to attend him to be ready by a short day.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume I, London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But, alas! he who escapes from death is not pardoned; he is only reprieved, and reprieved to a short day.

definitions.definition: (finance) Being in a financial investment position that is structured to be profitable if the price of the underlying security declines in the future.
(by extension) Doubtful of, skeptical of.
(finance, dated) Of money: given in the fewest possible notes, i.e. those of the largest denomination.

quote.citation: 1909, James Blyth, The member for Easterby, page 296:
quote.text: He pulled a cheque-book from his pocket, and drew for two hundred thousand pounds. “I'll take it short,” he said  […]

definitions.definition: Abruptly, curtly, briefly.
Unawares.
Without achieving a goal or requirement.
(cricket, of the manner of bounce of a cricket ball) Relatively far from the batsman and hence bouncing higher than normal; opposite of full.
(finance) With a negative ownership position.
A short circuit.
A YouTube video that is less than one minute long.
A short-form vertical video.
A short film.

quote.citation: 2012 July 12, Sam Adams, AV Club, Ice Age: Continental Drift‎[2]:
quote.text: Preceded by a Simpsons short shot in 3-D—perhaps the only thing more superfluous than a fourth Ice Age movie—Ice Age: Continental Drift finds a retinue of vaguely contemporaneous animals coping with life in the post-Pangaea age.

definitions.definition: A short version of a garment in a particular size.
(baseball) A shortstop.
(finance) A short seller.
(finance) A short sale or short position.
A summary account.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: For the short and the long is, our play is preferred.

definitions.definition: (phonetics) A short sound, syllable, or vowel.

quote.citation: 1877, Henry Sweet, A Handbook of Phonetics, page 18:
quote.text: If we compare the nearest conventional shorts and longs in English, as in ‘bit’ and ‘beat’, ‘not’ and ‘naught’, we find that the short vowels are generally wide (i, ɔ), the long narrow (i, ɔ), besides being generally diphthongic as well.

definitions.definition: (programming) An integer variable having a smaller range than normal integers; usually two bytes long.
(US, slang) An automobile; especially in crack shorts, to break into automobiles.

quote.citation: 1975, Mary Sanches, Ben G. Blount, Sociocultural Dimensions of Language Use, page 47:
quote.text: For example, one addict would crack shorts (break and enter cars) and usually obtain just enough stolen goods to buy stuff and get off just before getting sick.

quote.citation: 1982, United States. Congress. Senate. Committee on the Judiciary. Subcommittee on Juvenile Justice, Career Criminal Life Sentence Act of 1981: Hearings, page 87:
quote.text: […]  list of all crimes reported by these 61 daily criminals during their years on the street is: theft (this includes shoplifting; "cracking shorts", burglary and other forms of stealing), dealing, forgery, gambling, confidence games (flim-flam, etc.)  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause a short circuit in (something).
(intransitive, of an electrical circuit) To short circuit.
(transitive, informal) To provide with an amount smaller than that agreed or labeled; to shortchange.

quote.citation: 1991 August 24, Maridee BonaDea, quoting Brian Freeman, “Pomo Afro Homos On The Road”, in Gay Community News, volume 19, number 6, page 9:
quote.text: It's hard now. The NEA, state and city budgets are messed up and it's the small artists like us that are the ones getting shorted.

definitions.definition: (transitive, business) To sell something, especially securities, that one does not own at the moment for delivery at a later date in hopes of profiting from a decline in the price; to sell short.
(obsolete) To shorten.
Deficient in.
(finance) Having a negative position in.

pronunciation: General Australian, New Zealand, Standard Southern British
